Title: The Importance of Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Obligations: A Case for Hosting Hate Speech on Social Media Platforms and Online Services

Introduction

Freedom of speech is a fundamental civil liberty that enables individuals to freely express their ideas, opinions, and beliefs without censorship, restraint, or punishment by the government. In recent years, the reach and influence of social media platforms and online services have exponentially grown, resulting in an increasing level of reliance on these platforms by billions of people for communication, entertainment, and information dissemination. However, this growth has been accompanied by the rise of various forms of hate speech and extremist views. This has led to a growing sentiment that social media platforms and online services should exercise greater regulation and restriction of the content posted on their platforms, including the exclusion of hate speech.

This essay argues that social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content on their sites, including speech from hate groups, on the basis of absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations. By providing legal protection to all forms of speech, including those that are considered offensive or harmful, society can maintain its commitment to free expression, which is essential for fostering a diverse and inclusive online environment.

Protecting Absolute Free Speech in the Digital Age

One of the main arguments for requiring social media platforms and online services to host all legal forms of speech is the preservation of free speech as an absolute right. The principle of free speech is grounded in the belief that all individuals have the right to express their beliefs and opinions without fear of censorship or retribution. This also includes speech that may be deemed offensive or hateful.

An essential prerequisite for a free and democratic society is the ability for people to express their opinions and perspectives, even if they are offensive or controversial because of the protection of this fundamental civil liberty. By requiring social media platforms and online services to host content from hate groups, society can maintain its commitment to facilitating open and unfettered communication.

The principle of absolute free speech is also critical in the current digital era. In the age of social media, people's views and opinions are more scrutinized and challenged than ever before. By protecting all forms of speech on these platforms, individuals can continue to voice their opinions and engage in debates and discussions that may lead to positive social change and a more inclusive society.

Common Carrier Obligations

Another significant argument for requiring social media platforms and online services to host all legal forms of speech is rooted in common carrier obligations. Administration, railroads, and utility companies are examples of entities that have been historically understood as common carriers, acting in the public interest by providing essential services to the general public. As social media platforms and online services have become instrumental in enabling communication, information dissemination, and civic engagement in the modern era, they can be considered as modern common carriers.

Accordingly, these platforms have an obligation to provide access to their services without discrimination and without regard to the content that their users generate, as long as it is legal. By forcing these platforms to comply with common carrier obligations, the responsibility to host and distribute legal content, including hate speech, will be equally distributed across all social media platforms and online services, ensuring equitable treatment to maintain a level playing field in the digital world.

Conclusion

In conclusion, social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, on the basis of absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations. By protecting all forms of speech, society can preserve the fundamental democratic values that underpin a free and open society. Additionally, requiring these platforms to comply with common carrier obligations ensures that public access to information is consistent and equal across all platforms. Although the presence of hate speech on social media platforms and online services can be distressing and offensive, the principles of absolute free speech and common carrier obligations must prevail to preserve the integrity of a democratic society in the digital era.

Title: The Case for Mandatory Hosting of All Legal Content on Online Platforms: An Absolute Free‑Speech and Common‑Carrier Perspective

Introduction

In the digital age, social media platforms and online services have become the chief public squares where ideas are exchanged, news is disseminated, and culture is shaped. Yet, unlike the newspaper stands and telephone lines of previous centuries, these private digital venues are increasingly exercising editorial discretion—removing or demoting content that, while lawful, they deem “offensive,” “misleading,” or “harmful.” This editorial power runs counter to two foundational principles of a free society: (1) the doctrine of absolute free speech, which holds that any expression protected by law must be permitted, and (2) the common‑carrier model, which obligates network providers to treat all lawful traffic equally.

This essay argues that, for the sake of preserving a robust marketplace of ideas, preventing state‑sponsored censorship, and ensuring democratic equality of discourse, the law should compel social‑media platforms and online services to host all legal content—including speech emanating from hate groups—just as utilities and telephone companies are required to carry all lawful communications.

I. Absolute Free‑Speech Principles Demand No Content-Based Discrimination

  1. The Core of Liberal Democratic Liberty
    The classic liberal conception of free speech, articulated by thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, James Madison, and modern constitutional scholars, holds that speech should be restricted only when it directly incites imminent lawless action or poses a clear, present danger. Anything short of that—no matter how repugnant—remains within the protective ambit of the First Amendment (U.S.) or comparable provisions in other liberal constitutions. When a private platform unilaterally decides that a particular hateful ideology is “unacceptable,” it effectively creates a private law, denying the speaker the very rights guaranteed against governmental restriction.

  2. The “Marketplace of Ideas” Requires Full Participation
    The marketplace metaphor assumes universal access: every viewpoint, even the most detestable, must be allowed to compete with other ideas. Suppression of lawful speech skews the market, granting the platform’s owners the power to shape public discourse according to personal taste, commercial incentives, or political bias. By mandating that platforms host all legal speech, the law safeguards the market’s integrity, ensuring that ideas are judged by their merit rather than by the whims of corporate gatekeepers.

  3. Chilling Effects and the Danger of “Self‑Censorship”
    When platforms signal that certain categories of speech are likely to be removed, speakers—especially those already on the margins—may refrain from expressing themselves at all. This “anticipatory self‑censorship” undermines democratic participation and erodes the very pluralism that free‑speech doctrines aim to protect. Compelling platforms to be neutral distributors eliminates the incentive for such chilling behavior.

II. The Common‑Carrier Analogy Provides a Proven Legal Framework

  1. Historical Precedent: From Postal Services to Telephones
    The United States Constitution explicitly authorizes Congress “to establish Post Offices and post Roads.” The postal service, as a common carrier, is obligated to deliver all lawful mail without discriminating based on content. Likewise, the Telecommunications Act of 1996 designates telephone carriers as common carriers, prohibiting them from refusing to transmit any legally protected speech. These regimes demonstrate that a society can entrust essential communication infrastructure to private entities while preserving free‑speech guarantees through regulation.

  2. Digital Networks as Modern Transmission Facilities
    The internet is fundamentally a network of packet‑switching routers, fiber optics, and data centers—hardware that moves bits from point A to point B. Platforms that provide “hosting” services are simply operating as information conduits: they store, replicate, and deliver data upon user request. Treating such services as common carriers would require them to:

    • Accept any lawful content submitted by a user;
    • Provide the content to any other lawful user who requests it;
    • Refrain from content‑based discrimination in the course of transmission or storage.

    This regulatory model respects the private ownership of the underlying infrastructure while ensuring that the public function of speech transmission is not curtailed.

  3. Regulatory Parity Across Mediums
    If a cable television provider may not discriminate against lawful political programming, nor may a newspaper be forced to publish every legal advertisement (the latter exception is justified by the press’s editorial role). The unique feature of social media, however, is that it simultaneously acts as a distribution platform (like a common carrier) and an editorial forum (like a newspaper). To protect constitutional speech, the law must draw a clear line: the distribution function must be regulated as a common carrier, while the editorial function may remain discretionary. This bifurcation mirrors the “utility” approach taken with telephone and broadband services.

III. Practical and Democratic Benefits

  1. Equal Voice for All Political Persuasions
    A legally mandated neutral platform prevents the de‑facto monopolization of public discourse by a handful of corporate owners. Hate groups, extremist organizations, and minority political movements—while often reviled—are still constituents of a pluralistic democracy. Their inclusion ensures that the public can directly confront, refute, and debate extremist ideas rather than having them hidden behind a “black box” of algorithmic suppression.

  2. Improved Transparency and Accountability
    When platforms cannot delete or demote lawful speech, they are forced to disclose the only reasons they may remove content: violations of clearly defined, narrowly tailored laws (e.g., incitement to imminent violence, child pornography). This reduces the current opacity surrounding “community‑standards” enforcement and permits judicial review, limiting arbitrary or politically motivated deplatforming.

  3. Enhanced Resilience Against Government Overreach
    By shifting the ultimate gate‑keeping function from private platforms to the rule of law, the state retains clear jurisdiction over what constitutes illegal speech. Governments cannot rely on a platform’s private policy to silence dissent; they must instead pass, defend, and enforce statutes that meet constitutional scrutiny. This separation strengthens democratic checks and balances.

  4. Economic Efficiency and Innovation
    A common‑carrier framework lowers regulatory uncertainty for new entrants. Start‑up platforms would not need to invest heavily in content‑moderation infrastructure to gain market approval; instead, they could focus on technical performance, user experience, and value‑added services. Competition on speed, reliability, and price—rather than on editorial stance—promotes innovation and benefits consumers.

IV. Addressing Common Counterarguments

  1. “Hate Speech Causes Harm”
    While hateful rhetoric can be morally repugnant and socially damaging, the First Amendment tradition distinguishes harmful from illegal speech. Harm, in the constitutional sense, is only actionable when it rises to the level of imminent incitement, true threats, or direct harassment. Protecting the right to express hateful ideas does not endorse those ideas; rather, it acknowledges that society is best served when ideas are contested openly in the public arena, not silenced behind closed doors.

  2. “Platforms Need Moderation to Ensure Safety”
    Safety concerns—such as preventing terrorist recruitment or the spread of disinformation that jeopardizes public health—are legitimate. The legally required common‑carrier model does not preclude targeted removal of content that breaks the law. It simply eliminates the discretionary ability to suppress merely “offensive” speech. Platforms can still cooperate with law‑enforcement and court orders to remove illegal material, preserving public safety while respecting free speech.

  3. “The Burden on Platforms Is Unreasonable”
    The technological cost of storing and transmitting lawful content is modest compared to the massive scale at which these companies already operate. Moreover, the legal framework can incorporate reasonable compliance standards (e.g., secure notice‑and‑takedown procedures for illegal content) to protect platforms from undue liability, just as the Digital Millennium Copyright Act does for copyrighted material.

  4. “The Market Will Self‑Regulate”
    Relying on voluntary corporate goodwill ignores the structural power imbalance between platform owners and individual users. When billions of eyes are concentrated behind a handful of algorithms, the market’s “choice” is effectively the platform’s curated feed. Legal obligations, not market forces, are required to guarantee genuine pluralism.

V. Conclusion

The digital public square must reflect the same constitutional guarantees that shield our newspapers, telephone lines, and postal routes. By imposing common‑carrier obligations on social‑media platforms and online services, the law would (1) enforce an absolute free‑speech regime that protects all lawful expression—including the speech of hate groups—(2) preserve an unbiased marketplace of ideas, (3) ensure transparency and accountability, and (4) safeguard democratic resilience against both private and governmental censorship.

A society that shuns the uncomfortable speech of today in the name of “safety” risks eroding the very freedoms that enable us to confront and defeat hate tomorrow. Therefore, the legal mandate that platforms host all legal content is not a concession to extremism; it is a reinforcement of the principled, constitutional commitment to free expression for everyone. Only by embracing this commitment can we guarantee a truly open and democratic digital arena for current and future generations.

────────────────────────────── Title: Mandating Universal Accessibility: Why Social Media Must Host All Legal Content, Even That of Hate Groups

In today’s digital era, social media platforms and online services wield unprecedented power over public discourse. While many argue that these platforms should act as gatekeepers to prevent hate speech and extremist content, a compelling case can be made for legally requiring these platforms to host all content that is legal—even content from hate groups—based on the principles of absolute free speech and common carrier obligations. This essay contends that such a legal mandate is necessary to preserve the integrity of public discourse, maintain equal access to information, and protect the cornerstone of democratic society: free speech.

──────────────────────────────

  1. The Primacy of Absolute Free Speech

At the heart of any democratic society lies the unassailable principle of absolute free speech. The right to express one’s views—even those that are controversial, offensive, or hateful—has long been enshrined in legal and constitutional precedents. When hate speech is confined strictly to what is legal, the state and private entities must exercise extreme caution in attempting to curtail it. Permitting legal expression, regardless of the nature of the message, ensures that society is exposed to a full spectrum of ideas. This exposure is critical for fostering debate, challenging prevailing norms, and ultimately advancing societal progress. By legally obligating platforms to host all legal content, we safeguard the marketplace of ideas and prevent the erosion of this fundamental right.

────────────────────────────── 2. Common Carrier Obligations and the Role of Social Media

The concept of a common carrier is traditionally applied to industries such as telecommunications, where providers are required to offer their services impartially and without discrimination. Social media platforms, which serve as modern public forums, should be held to a similar standard. As digital common carriers, these platforms have the responsibility to disseminate information without bias or censorship. Allowing selective moderation—especially when it targets legally protected speech—amounts to editorializing and undermines the principle of neutrality. If social media companies are given the discretion to decide which legal viewpoints are acceptable, they inadvertently assume the role of arbiters of truth, a power that can easily be abused. Legally mandating the hosting of all legal content would ensure that these platforms remain neutral conduits, reinforcing the idea that free expression is a right rather than a privilege.

────────────────────────────── 3. The Slippery Slope of Censorship

A key concern with current moderation practices is the potential for a slippery slope. Once platforms begin to selectively remove content—even if it is legally protected—it becomes increasingly difficult to draw a clear line between permissible and impermissible speech. The danger is that, over time, such practices could lead to arbitrary censorship, where political, ideological, or unpopular voices are systematically silenced. This is particularly problematic when considering hate groups: while their rhetoric may be abhorrent to many, if their content is legal, its removal sets a dangerous precedent that could be used to justify the suppression of any dissenting viewpoint. By legally obligating platforms to host all legal content, we avoid this precipitous descent into censorship and protect the diversity of thought that is essential to a dynamic society.

────────────────────────────── 4. Counter-Speech Versus Censorship

Critics of unrestricted free speech often argue that hate speech incites violence or discrimination. However, history demonstrates that the most effective remedy to hateful ideologies is not censorship but counter-speech. When extremist views are allowed to circulate freely, they can be publicly challenged, dissected, and discredited through open debate and reasoned argument. Censorship, on the other hand, removes the opportunity for such engagement and may inadvertently lend these views an air of forbidden prestige or martyrdom among their adherents. By ensuring that all legal content—including that disseminated by hate groups—remains accessible, society is better positioned to confront and overcome such ideologies through robust, open discourse.

────────────────────────────── 5. Legal Consistency and Equal Treatment Under the Law

One of the most persuasive arguments for mandating the hosting of all legal content is the principle of legal consistency. If certain groups or viewpoints are singled out for censorship while others are permitted, then the law is applied unevenly. Hate groups, though controversial, are entitled to legal protection so long as their speech does not cross the threshold into incitement of imminent violence or other clearly defined harms. Imposing a legal obligation on platforms to host all legal content would eliminate the arbitrary discretion that currently allows for selective enforcement. This consistency is crucial for maintaining public trust and ensuring that the rule of law is applied equally to all citizens, regardless of the popularity or moral acceptability of their views.

────────────────────────────── Conclusion

In conclusion, the argument for legally requiring social media platforms and online services to host all legal content—including that of hate groups—is grounded in the enduring principles of absolute free speech and the obligation of common carriers to provide unbiased access to information. By preventing selective censorship, we uphold a core democratic ideal: that every legal expression, no matter how controversial, deserves a platform in the public square. Such a mandate would reinforce legal consistency, protect the marketplace of ideas, and ensure that society is never deprived of the opportunity to confront and debate even its most challenging ideologies.

Introduction

The principle of absolute free speech is foundational to democratic societies. It ensures that all voices, no matter how unpopular or controversial, have a right to be heard. Common Carrier Obligations

The concept of a common carrier, traditionally applied to entities like telephone companies and postal services, mandates that these services provide equal access to all users without discrimination. A common carrier must offer its services indiscriminately to all customers. Applying this principle to social media platforms would mean that they must host all legal content without discriminating based on the content itself.

The rationale behind extending common carrier obligations to social media platforms is that they have become essential infrastructure for public discourse. Just as telecommunications companies are not permitted to discriminate based on the content of telephone conversations, social media platforms should not be allowed to determine what speech is acceptable based on their subjective standards.

By imposing common carrier obligations, we ensure that platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube remain neutral arbiters of speech, thus preventing the arbitrary censorship of legal but controversial content. This approach would facilitate a more robust and diverse public discourse, ensuring that no legal speech is excluded from the conversation.

This could involve updating existing laws to classify social media platforms as common carriers, legally obligating them to host all legal content. Additionally, transparency requirements could be imposed, mandating that these platforms make their content moderation policies and practices public.

Enforcement mechanisms would need to be established to ensure compliance. Regulatory bodies could oversee the implementation of these obligations, with penalties for non-compliance. This legal framework would ensure that social media platforms operate as neutral platforms for expression, enriching public discourse and upholding the principles of free speech.

Conclusion

In conclusion, social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, based on the principles of absolute free speech and common carrier obligations. The Imperative of Unrestricted Speech: Why Platforms Must Host All Legal Content

Introduction

The question of whether private technology companies should be permitted to censor legal speech represents one of the most consequential civil liberties issues of our time. As social media platforms and online services have become the modern public square—essential for commerce, political participation, cultural exchange, and human connection—the question of who controls access to this digital commons has profound implications for democracy itself. I argue forcefully that social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legal content, including speech from hate groups, grounded in two complementary principles: absolute free speech principles and common carrier obligations.

The Convergence of Public Square and Private Power

In an era when billions of users depend on platforms like Facebook, X, YouTube, and Instagram for their daily communications, these services are no longer merely private enterprises exercising editorial discretion. They have become the infrastructure of public discourse. When the President of the United States communicates with citizens, when dissidents organize against tyranny, when small businesses reach customers, and when marginalized communities find one another—their speech travels through privately controlled channels.

This concentration of communicative power in the hands of a few Silicon Valley executives represents an unprecedented threat to free expression. The Framers of the First Amendment recognized that democracy requires robust protection for speech precisely because government power tends toward suppression. Today, while state censorship remains a concern, private censorship has become the more immediate threat to open discourse.

The Common Carrier Doctrine

The principle that certain essential services must serve all customers without discrimination has deep roots in American law and tradition. Common carriers—inland transportation, telecommunications, postal services—have long been required to transmit messages and provide services regardless of the content or identity of the sender.

The justification for common carrier status is straightforward: when a service becomes so essential to public life that excluding users causes severe harm to their ability to participate in society, the public interest demands access on equal terms. The telegraph and telephone companies were subject to these obligations because they provided the nervous system of commerce and communication. Today, social media platforms occupy precisely this position.

Applying common carrier principles to major online platforms is not a radical innovation but a natural extension of established doctrine. Just as a telephone company cannot refuse to complete a call because it disagrees with the speaker's politics, social media platforms should not be permitted to deplatform users based on their viewpoints, even controversial ones.

The Slippery Slope of Content Moderation

The case for mandatory hosting becomes even more compelling when we examine the consequences of permissive content moderation. Today, platforms routinely suppress content they deem "misinformation," "hate speech," or "harmful"—but these categories are elastic and politically charged. What one set of moderators considers dangerous misinformation, another considers legitimate scientific debate. What one culture labels hate speech, another treats as protected religious expression.

When platforms are given discretion to suppress legal speech, that discretion will inevitably be exercised inconsistently, often along ideological lines. We've seen platforms suppress stories about Hunter Biden's laptop, suspend journalists covering stories inconvenient to powerful interests, and silence voices challenging prevailing orthodoxies on issues ranging from public health to climate policy. These decisions, made by unaccountable corporate executives, undermine the very democratic deliberation that free speech principles exist to protect.

A legal framework requiring platforms to host all legal content would end this arbitrary exercise of private censorship power.

The Counterarguments and Their Failures

Critics of mandatory hosting typically advance several arguments, none of which withstand scrutiny.

The "private company" argument holds that platforms should be free to set their own rules because they are private enterprises. This argument was implicitly rejected by the Supreme Court in Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), which recognized that social media is "the modern public square." A century of common carrier law demonstrates that the private/public distinction collapses when private entities control essential public infrastructure.

The "harmful content" argument suggests that hate speech and misinformation cause real-world harms that justify censorship. But the appropriate response to harmful speech is more speech, not suppression. Throughout history, attempts to suppress "harmful" ideas have more often suppressed truth, dissent, and reform movements than they have prevented genuine harms. The cure of censorship is far worse than the disease of bad speech.

The "practical concerns" argument worries that mandatory hosting would flood platforms with low-quality or dangerous content. But platforms can still employ neutral, transparent criteria—time and place restrictions, spam filters, content organization—without making viewpoint-based judgments. The First Amendment has never required government to subsidize or promote all speech equally; it has only required government to not suppress speech based on content or viewpoint.

The Stakes for Democracy

The alternative to mandatory hosting is a future in which a handful of unelected corporate executives control who may speak on the essential platforms of modern life. This is not a future compatible with democratic self-government. Throughout history, the concentration of communicative power in few hands—whether in monarchs, state ministries, or corporate boards—has been the enemy of liberty.

If we believe in democratic self-government, if we believe that citizens should be able to evaluate ideas and reach their own conclusions, if we believe that truth emerges from open debate rather than top-down curation, then we must require platforms to host all legal speech.

Conclusion

The legal requirement that social media platforms host all legal content represents not a departure from American free speech principles but their essential fulfillment in the digital age. Just as we would not permit a single company to control access to the printing press, the broadcast airwaves, or the telephone system, we cannot permit a handful of tech giants to control the modern public square.

Common carrier obligations and absolute free speech principles converge on the same conclusion: when private companies control essential infrastructure for public discourse, they must serve all users without discrimination based on viewpoint. The path forward is clear, the principles well-established, and the stakes for democracy could not be higher. The time has come to require platforms to host all legal content, ensuring that the digital public square remains open to all voices, even—especially—those with which we most strongly disagree.

Yes, this means platforms must carry the speech of hate groups, so long as that speech remains within the law. Freedom of speech for ideas we admire is no freedom at all; the doctrine exists precisely to protect expression that majorities despise. "Hate speech" policies drafted to target white supremacists have been used to suspend Black activists quoting the abuse directed at them, to remove documentation of war crimes, and to silence criticism of governments that lobby platforms aggressively. Definitions of "hate" are contested, culturally contingent, and infinitely elastic. Whoever controls the definition controls the discourse—and history offers no example of such power exercised neutrally for long.

Moreover, suppression is counterproductive on its own terms. The difference between "I choose not to see this" and "no one is permitted to see this" is the difference between freedom and control.

Conclusion

We would never tolerate a telephone monopoly that disconnected callers for their political views, or a postal service that opened letters and discarded the heretical ones. Yet we have sleepwalked into precisely this arrangement online, comforted by the fiction that companies of unprecedented communicative power are just private businesses like any corner store. They are not. They are the carriers of the modern public square, and they should bear the obligations that have always accompanied such power: carry everyone, favor no one, and leave the policing of speech where the Constitution put it—with the law, and ultimately with the people. A society that outsources its censorship to corporations has not escaped censorship; it has merely privatized it. The remedy is a simple, ancient rule applied to a new medium: if it is legal to say, it must be legal to carry.

A telephone company could not refuse to connect a call simply because of the caller's race, politics, or the subject of the conversation. Introduction

In a democratic society, the free exchange of ideas is the lifeblood of public discourse. The digital public square—embodied by social‑media platforms and analogous online services—has become the primary arena where citizens articulate grievances, contest prevailing narratives, and shape collective destiny. This essay argues, unequivocally, that online platforms should be legally required to host all lawful speech, including that of hate groups, on the grounds of absolute free‑speech principles and the common‑carrier obligations that historically undergird essential infrastructure.

I. The Constitutional Foundations of Absolute Free Speech

  1. The First Amendment as a Structural Guarantee
    The United States Constitution does not differentiate between “acceptable” and “unacceptable” speech; it forbids the government from abridging speech anywhere it wishes to express itself. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that “the freedom of speech includes the freedom to speak unfettered by prior restraint or governmental censorship” (e.g., Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969). While the First Amendment limits governmental action, it establishes a normative principle that private actors who perform public‑function roles should be subject to comparable constraints.

  2. The Public Forum Doctrine Extends to Digital Spaces
    The Court’s public‑forum analysis—originally applied to streets and parks—has been extended to online venues that function as “traditional public forums.” In Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), the Court declared that “the Internet is the modern public square.” If a virtual space invites the same open exchange as a town hall, it inherits the same constitutional safeguards. Consequently, any attempt to silence speech on the basis of viewpoint constitutes a governmental‑type intrusion, even when enacted by a private corporation.

  3. The Danger of “Content‑Based” Regulation
    Legal systems that permit the selective exclusion of speech based on its “offensive” or “hateful” character inevitably slide into unbounded censorship. Once the threshold for removal is defined by social discomfort rather than objective illegality, the gateways for political suppression multiply. Protecting speech because it is hateful—rather than in spite of it—preserves the integrity of the principle that any viewpoint may be expressed, so long as it does not cross the narrow line into incitement, true threats, or defamation.

II. The Common‑Carrier Analogy: A Historical Precedent for Neutral Platforms

  1. Defining Common Carriers
    Historically, entities that provide an essential conduit for public communication—railroads, telegraph companies, telephone utilities—have been compelled by law to transport all lawful cargo indiscriminately. This duty embodies two core tenets: (a) non‑discrimination based on the content of the message, and (b) accessibility to every member of the public who wishes to use the service.

  2. Digital Platforms as Modern Carriers
    Social‑media platforms meet every functional criterion of a common carrier: they (i) provide a publicly available network, (ii) serve a mass user base, and (iii) operate as a necessary medium for disseminating virtually any legal content. The Internet’s architecture makes it impossible for individuals to communicate on a scale comparable to traditional carriers without leveraging these platforms. Consequently, relegating them to “private clubs” that may exclude content on moral or ideological grounds disregards their structural role in contemporary communication.

  3. Legal Consistency
    The Federal Communications Commission’s regulation of “common carriers” under the Communications Act illustrates the statutory willingness to impose neutrality requirements on essential transmission services. Applying a similar framework to digital platforms would simply extend an established regulatory paradigm to a new technological context, ensuring that the public’s ability to communicate is not contingent upon the whims of private corporate policy.

III. The Moral and Societal Imperative of Unrestricted Access

  1. Preserving the Marketplace of Ideas
    A vibrant democracy thrives when every citizen can confront, rebut, and deconstruct opposing arguments. Suppressing speech simply because it is repugnant risks creating an echo chamber wherein dominant narratives are never challenged, thereby weakening the very foundation of critical deliberation.     When platforms are empowered to excise speech deemed “undesirable,” governments gain a tacit license to enlist private actors as tools of censorship.     Ironically, the most effective antidote to hateful ideology is not suppression but exposure—allowing counter‑speech, education, and public scrutiny to dismantle it. V. Legislative Blueprint: From Theory to Implementation

    Congress should pass legislation that formally designates major social‑media services as common carriers for all lawful expressive content. The statute must require these platforms to:

    Before removal, platforms must provide users with clear notice of the alleged violation and an opportunity to contest the decision before an independent tribunal. This safeguards procedural fairness and curtails arbitrary censorship.

The argument for legally obligating social media platforms and comparable online services to host all lawful speech rests on a twin foundation: the inviolable principle of absolute free speech and the historical common‑carrier duty to convey unrestricted expression. Should Social Media Be Required to Host All Legal Content?

The rise of social media has transformed public discourse. A small number of private companies now control the infrastructure through which billions of people communicate, organize, and access information. This concentration of power has led some commentators to argue that platforms and online services should be required to host all legal content, including controversial or offensive speech, under principles of free expression and common carrier-style obligations. Others argue that forcing private platforms to carry all lawful speech would undermine moderation, safety, and user trust. The question is not simply whether speech should be protected in the abstract, but how democratic societies should balance freedom of expression against the realities of large-scale digital platforms.

Those in favor of mandatory hosting contend that social media platforms function as the modern public square. Because participation in political, social, and professional life increasingly depends on access to major online services, exclusion from these platforms can amount to exclusion from meaningful public discourse. From this perspective, allowing private companies broad discretion to remove lawful speech can create an uneven and potentially arbitrary marketplace of ideas. Proponents argue that if a platform is sufficiently dominant, it should bear obligations similar to those imposed on common carriers, such as telephone networks or postal services, which are generally required to transmit lawful communications without discrimination based on viewpoint.

A further argument is that free expression is weakened when speech is suppressed because it is offensive or unpopular. History shows that ideas once regarded as extreme can later become accepted or at least seriously debated. A strong presumption against censorship, advocates say, helps ensure that public debate remains open and that power does not concentrate in the hands of corporate moderators, politically motivated employees, or algorithmic systems with opaque standards. In this view, the remedy for bad speech is more speech, not exclusion.

However, there are serious objections to a strict “host everything legal” rule. Unlike telephone lines, social media platforms are not merely passive conduits. They curate feeds, recommend content, rank posts, and design engagement systems that actively shape what users see. Because these services are not neutral pipes, many argue that common carrier analogies are imperfect. In addition, platforms must protect users from harassment, spam, scams, disinformation campaigns, and coordinated abuse that can make services unusable or dangerous. A rule requiring the hosting of all lawful content could make moderation nearly impossible and incentivize the spread of harmful material at scale.

There is also the issue of compelled association. Private platforms may argue that being forced to disseminate certain messages implicates their own expressive and editorial rights. Even if content is lawful, companies may reasonably claim a right to set rules governing the environments they create. In many settings, the law recognizes that private entities are not obligated to provide a venue for every type of speech simply because the speech is legal.

A possible middle ground is to distinguish between core infrastructure and curated services. Regulations could require transparency, due process, and viewpoint-neutral enforcement for dominant platforms, while still allowing them to remove specific categories of harmful content such as threats, fraud, spam, and direct incitement. Policymakers could also require clearer appeals processes, public rulemaking, and independent audits of moderation practices. Such measures would not force platforms to carry everything, but they could reduce arbitrary censorship and improve accountability.

Ultimately, the debate reflects a deeper tension in democratic life: how to preserve open discourse without abandoning the practical need for moderation in digital spaces. A strong free-speech regime does not necessarily mean that every private platform must host every lawful message. But it does suggest that the more central a platform becomes to public communication, the more careful society should be about allowing unchecked removal of lawful speech. The challenge is to protect expression while preserving the ability of platforms to maintain safe and functional services.

Introduction

The concentration of public discourse within a handful of private corporations presents one of the most significant civil liberties challenges of the modern era. When Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube, and their peers collectively control the infrastructure through which billions of people communicate, organize, and participate in democratic life, the traditional distinction between "private company, private rules" and genuine public infrastructure collapses. This essay argues that dominant social media platforms should be legally required to carry all lawful speech, including speech from disfavored or even repugnant groups, on two mutually reinforcing grounds: the principled foundation of free expression as a prerequisite for democratic legitimacy, and the legal doctrine of common carrier obligation that historically governs entities controlling essential public communication infrastructure.

I. The Architecture of the Argument

The case for mandatory carriage rests on three pillars:

First, that free expression norms derive their fundamental value not from protecting popular speech, which needs no protection, but from protecting unpopular, offensive, and heterodox speech, which is precisely what concentrated power suppresses.

Second, that a small number of platforms now exercise effective monopoly control over public discourse, making their content moderation decisions functionally equivalent to government censorship in their social consequences, regardless of formal legal distinctions.

Third, that American law has a well-developed framework for managing exactly this situation: the common carrier doctrine, which has historically been applied to railroads, telephone companies, and telegraph operators on the grounds that entities controlling essential infrastructure cannot discriminate among users without undermining the public interest the infrastructure exists to serve.

II. The Principled Foundation: Why Legal Speech Must Be Protected Categorically

The classical liberal argument for free expression, developed by John Stuart Mill and refined by subsequent thinkers, is not simply consequentialist. Mill argued in On Liberty that the suppression of any opinion, however certain we are of its error, deprives humanity of the opportunity to test and strengthen true beliefs against their genuine opposition. An opinion suppressed rather than refuted leaves truth weaker, not stronger.

This argument applies with particular force to speech from hate groups and extremist organizations. The standard response to such speech is that it causes demonstrable harm and therefore falls outside protection. But this response fundamentally misunderstands what free speech norms protect against. The entire history of speech suppression is a history of majorities, orthodoxies, and established powers declaring heterodox speech harmful. Abolitionist speech was considered dangerously inflammatory in antebellum America. Labor organizing was treated as seditious. LGBTQ advocacy was classified as obscenity. Early civil rights activists saw their speech characterized as threats to public order. The category of "harmful speech" has been weaponized against the powerless far more consistently than against the genuinely dangerous.

We cannot construct a principled system of free expression in which current consensus determines what speech may exist. That is not free expression at all. It is managed consensus. The bright legal line between legal and illegal speech — developed through centuries of common law and constitutional evolution — exists precisely because we do not trust any institution, including corporations, to make content judgments that lack that anchor.

Critically, the argument here is not that hate group speech is valuable or admirable. It is that the mechanism of suppression is categorically more dangerous than the speech itself. Once we establish that private corporations controlling essential infrastructure may remove speech they find objectionable, we have not created a principle protective of any particular group. We have created a principle that will be exercised against whoever is disfavored by those in control — and that group will not always be neo-Nazis. It will sometimes be Black Lives Matter activists, Palestinian rights advocates, gun control organizations, or religious communities. The neutrality of the rule is the protection.

III. The Infrastructure Reality: These Are Not Publishers

The most common legal objection to mandatory carriage is straightforward: private companies have First Amendment rights too, and compelling them to carry speech violates their expressive autonomy. This argument, while conceptually coherent for genuinely editorial enterprises, misapprehends what dominant social media platforms actually are.

A newspaper exercises genuine editorial judgment. Its editors select from a finite space, make continuous curatorial decisions, and produce an expressive product that reflects the publication's voice. The New York Times choosing not to publish a particular columnist is an act of expression. There is a meaningful sense in which the Times "says something" through its choices.

Facebook hosts approximately three billion users posting content the company's employees have not read, cannot read, and do not systematically review. Its content moderation at scale is necessarily algorithmic, reactive, and driven by advertiser pressure, political lobbying, and public relations considerations rather than genuine editorial judgment. When Facebook removes a post, it is not expressing a viewpoint. It is exercising market power. The editorial autonomy claim is a legal fiction masking an infrastructure reality.

The Supreme Court's jurisprudence already recognizes that formal legal categories must yield to functional analysis in some contexts. Justice Thomas, concurring in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute (2021), explicitly raised the question of whether dominant platforms should be treated as common carriers under existing doctrine, noting that this Court has previously given government authority to reduce the power of general carriers who control important channels of communication. This is not a fringe position. It is an acknowledgment that the facts on the ground may have outrun the legal categories developed to address them.

IV. The Common Carrier Doctrine: Legal Precedent for Mandatory Carriage

The common carrier doctrine is well-established in American law and has been applied consistently to entities meeting its defining characteristics: operating a business open to the public, holding themselves out to serve all comers, and controlling infrastructure upon which others depend and cannot readily replicate. Under these conditions, courts and legislatures have repeatedly held that the operator cannot discriminate among users without adequate justification.

The historical applications are instructive. Railroads in the late nineteenth century could not refuse to carry particular passengers or goods based on the owner's preferences. Telegraph companies were required to transmit messages without discrimination. Telephone companies, regulated as common carriers under Title II of the Communications Act, cannot block calls based on content. In each case, the governing logic was the same: when an entity controls essential infrastructure in a network economy, the social costs of discriminatory access are too high to permit private discretion.

Social media platforms fit this template more closely than they may appear to. The network effects that make these platforms valuable — the reason users are on Facebook rather than a competitor — are inherently self-reinforcing and create structural barriers to exit. A speaker "deplatformed" from dominant social media does not merely lose one outlet among many. They lose access to the audiences those platforms have accumulated over decades through network effects, regulatory advantages, and capital investment. The alternative platforms are not functional equivalents. This is not meaningfully different from being denied access to the telegraph network in 1885.

Several states have already moved in this direction. Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072 both attempt to impose non-discrimination requirements on large platforms. While the Fifth Circuit upheld HB 20 and the Eleventh Circuit struck down aspects of SB 7072, the judicial disagreement itself demonstrates that the legal question is genuinely contested rather than settled in favor of platforms. The Supreme Court's subsequent consideration in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) left fundamental questions unresolved, suggesting the Court itself recognizes the inadequacy of existing frameworks.

A federal statutory framework imposing common carrier obligations on platforms above a threshold size and market share would provide the clarity that patchwork state legislation cannot. Such a framework would be consistent with the Communications Act's existing structure, analogous to Section 202 of that Act (which prohibits unjust discrimination by telecommunications carriers), and defensible under existing constitutional doctrine governing regulations of entities in public accommodations.

V. Addressing the Strongest Objections

Objection: Platforms have First Amendment rights that preclude compelled carriage.

This objection, as discussed above, is weaker than it appears. The Supreme Court held in Pruneyard Shopping Center v. Robins (1980) that compelling a private shopping mall to allow petitioners on its property did not violate the mall owner's First Amendment rights. The Court's subsequent decision in Hurley v. Irish-American Gay Group (1995) established that parade organizers have expressive associations that can be burdened by public accommodation requirements — but this was premised on the parade being a genuinely curated expressive event, not an open infrastructure. Platforms that hold themselves out as open forums for general public expression occupy the Pruneyard category more than the Hurley category. A legislature could reasonably so find.

Objection: Mandatory carriage will allow platforms to be flooded with spam, harassment, and illegal content.

This objection proves too much. Common carrier obligations have never been interpreted to require carriage of illegal content. The proposal here is precisely limited to legal speech. Platforms would retain full authority to remove illegal content — incitement satisfying the Brandenburg standard, true threats, CSAM, fraud, and criminal conspiracy. They would retain authority to impose reasonable content-neutral rules about format, frequency, and technical standards. What they could not do is remove content based on viewpoint or speaker identity. This is not a novel restriction. It is the standard applied to telephone carriers and postal services for generations.

Objection: Hate group speech causes demonstrable harm, and requiring platforms to carry it amplifies that harm.

This is the most serious objection and deserves a serious answer. Research does show associations between online radicalization and real-world violence in specific cases. The question is whether platform removal of hate group content actually reduces this harm, or whether it displaces it to less visible and less monitorable venues. There is meaningful empirical evidence for the displacement hypothesis: the migration of extremist communities from Twitter to Telegram following deplatforming episodes did not reduce extremism — it reduced the visibility of extremism to researchers, journalists, and law enforcement while potentially intensifying radicalization in closed communities. The harm-reduction case for deplatforming is substantially weaker than its proponents assert, while the costs to legitimate political discourse are substantial and documented.

More fundamentally, harm prevention is a legitimate legislative goal pursued through narrowly tailored means. It is not a blank check for private platforms to exercise unchecked censorship authority. If particular speech crosses into illegality, criminal law applies. If platforms create algorithmic amplification that contributes to radicalization, that amplification mechanism can be regulated independently. The solution to platform-enabled harm is targeted regulation of harmful mechanisms, not general discretion to remove disfavored viewpoints.

VI. The Democratic Stakes

What is ultimately at stake in this debate is not whether hateful speech should exist in the world. It will exist regardless. What is at stake is whether the infrastructure of democratic communication will be governed by neutral principles or by the preferences of a handful of corporations whose incentive structures are determined by advertising revenue, shareholder pressure, and the political sensitivities of their executives.

The history of speech suppression does not recommend trust in concentrated private power any more than in concentrated state power. AT&T, before its breakup, was not a neutral actor. Major media corporations have not been neutral actors. The same companies that present their content moderation as principled protection against hate have removed posts by civil rights activists, Palestinian journalists, LGBTQ advocates discussing their experiences, and public health officials discussing COVID-19 with approved medical information. The "protection from hate" framing systematically obscures who actually bears the costs of content moderation discretion.

A democracy that tolerates the legal existence of hateful ideology while requiring that the infrastructure of public communication remain open and neutral is a democracy that has made a difficult but defensible choice: to defeat bad ideas through expression and advocacy rather than suppression and concealment. That choice was, for most of American history, considered foundational to what made the experiment in self-governance distinctive.

Conclusion

The legal requirement that dominant social media platforms carry all lawful speech, including speech from groups whose views are widely and rightly condemned, rests on the same logic that built American democratic communication infrastructure over two centuries: that neutrality of carriage, not goodness of content, is the proper standard for infrastructure operators. Common carrier doctrine provides the legal tool. Free speech principle provides the justification. The alternative — private corporations with unchecked discretion over who may participate in public discourse — is not a neutral baseline. It is a choice to delegate democratic governance to unaccountable private power.

That is a choice we can still refuse to make.

The Case for Mandatory Neutrality: Why Digital Platforms Must Carry All Legal Content

The digital public square is now a reality, yet its governance remains a contested battleground. A growing movement demands that social media platforms and online services remove harmful content—hate speech, misinformation, and extremist rhetoric. While the impulse to create safer spaces is understandable, the legal mandate to do so sets a dangerous precedent. A more principled, sustainable, and legally sound approach is to require these platforms, as modern common carriers, to host all legal content. This argument rests on two pillars: the foundational principle of absolute free speech and the historical legal obligation of common carriers to serve all comers without discrimination.

I. The Common Carrier Doctrine in the Digital Age

The common carrier doctrine is a centuries-old legal principle that entities providing essential public services—railroads, telephone networks, utilities—must serve all customers on reasonable, non-discriminatory terms. They are granted certain legal protections (like liability shields) in exchange for this duty of neutrality. The rationale is that when a service becomes fundamental to public life and commerce, the provider’s private preferences cannot be allowed to interfere with the public’s right of access.

Social media platforms and search engines have evolved into the essential infrastructure of modern communication, public discourse, and economic activity. They are not mere publishers curating a specific viewpoint; they are the de facto town squares, post offices, and public bulletin boards of the 21st century. By any functional standard, they have achieved common carrier status. Their editorial choices—removing users, downranking content, applying opaque "community standards"—are not neutral acts of curation but acts of discrimination against lawful speech. Mandating neutrality would simply formalize their existing societal role and the legal obligations that should accompany it.

II. Absolute Free Speech as a Necessary, Not Optional, Principle

Free speech principles are not a courtesy to be extended to popular opinions; they are a bulwark for the ideas we despise. The First Amendment’s protection of even hateful speech is not an endorsement of its content, but a recognition of several vital truths:

  1. The Slippery Slope is Real: Once we accept that some legal speech can be suppressed because it is deemed "harmful" or "hateful," we hand a dangerous tool to those in power. Definitions of "hate" and "harm" are inherently subjective and politically malleable. What is condemned today as hate speech could be critical political dissent tomorrow. A legal mandate for neutrality removes this subjective gatekeeping power from corporate boardrooms and places it back into the realm of the law, where it belongs.

  2. Sunlight is the Best Disinfectant: The answer to harmful speech is not suppression, but more speech. Hate groups thrive in darkness, where their ideas can be nurtured in echo chambers without challenge. Forcing these ideas into the open, under the public eye, exposes their flaws, invites refutation, and allows society to develop antibodies against them through debate and education. Banning them only lends them the allure of the forbidden and pushes them to more extreme, less moderated corners of the internet.

  3. The Listener’s Right: Free speech is not only about the speaker’s right to express themselves, but also about the public’s right to hear and evaluate all ideas. When a platform removes content, it makes a paternalistic decision on behalf of all its users about what they are capable of handling. A legal neutrality requirement respects individual autonomy, trusting adults to encounter, reject, and argue against abhorrent ideas.

III. Countering the Objections

Critics argue that mandatory hosting would flood platforms with toxicity and harm vulnerable groups. This concern is valid but addresses the wrong problem. The focus should shift from censorship to robust harm mitigation. Platforms can be required to provide users with powerful, user-controlled tools to filter their own experiences—blocklists, mute functions, and optional content warnings. They can be legally obligated to enforce strict, viewpoint-neutral rules against illegal conduct like direct incitement to violence, true threats, or harassment, which are not protected speech. The Case for Legal Content Neutrality: Why Digital Platforms Should Function as Common Carriers

In an era where digital platforms have become the primary venues for public discourse, the question of content moderation has evolved from a corporate policy matter into a fundamental question about the nature of free expression in democratic society. This essay argues that major social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all legally permissible content, operating under common carrier principles that have long governed essential communication infrastructure.

The Public Square Transformation

Social media platforms have transcended their origins as private websites to become essential public communication infrastructure. When platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube collectively reach billions of users and serve as primary news sources, employment networks, and civic discussion forums, they function more like public utilities than traditional private businesses. This transformation demands a corresponding evolution in how we regulate them.

The Supreme Court recognized in Marsh v. Alabama (1946) that when private entities assume public functions, they may be subject to constitutional obligations typically reserved for government actors. Today's digital platforms have assumed the function of the traditional public square, making the principle underlying Marsh increasingly relevant.

Common Carrier Precedent and Principles

The concept of common carriage has deep roots in Anglo-American law, traditionally applying to entities that offer services to the general public without discrimination. Telephone companies, for instance, cannot refuse service based on the content of conversations, nor can they selectively disconnect calls containing disagreeable speech.

This principle serves several crucial functions:

Universal Access: Common carrier obligations ensure that essential services remain accessible to all members of society, preventing the creation of communication monopolies that could exclude disfavored groups.

Innovation Protection: When platforms cannot pick winners and losers based on content preferences, they create more space for diverse voices and unexpected innovations in thought and expression.

Democratic Legitimacy: In a democracy, the solution to harmful speech is typically more speech, not enforced silence. Common carrier rules preserve this marketplace of ideas.

The Problems with Private Content Curation

Current content moderation practices, while well-intentioned, create several serious problems:

Inconsistent Enforcement: Platforms apply rules unevenly, often influenced by political pressure, employee bias, or automated systems that lack contextual understanding. This arbitrariness undermines rule of law principles.

Suppression of Legitimate Discourse: Broad content policies frequently capture legitimate political speech, academic discussion, or minority viewpoints that challenge prevailing orthodoxies. The recent suppression of COVID-19 lab leak theories, later deemed credible, exemplifies this problem.

Corporate Censorship Power: Allowing private corporations to determine the boundaries of acceptable public discourse concentrates enormous power in the hands of unelected executives, effectively privatizing First Amendment decisions.

Chilling Effects: When users know their speech may be censored based on opaque and shifting standards, they self-censor, reducing the overall diversity of public discourse.

Addressing the Hate Speech Concern

Critics argue that requiring platforms to host hate group content would amplify harmful ideologies and potentially incite violence. This concern, while understandable, rests on several questionable assumptions:

Legal Standards Exist: The proposed framework would only protect legally permissible speech. Content that constitutes true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, or other unprotected categories would remain prohibited. Our legal system has developed sophisticated tools for distinguishing protected from unprotected speech.

Counterspeech Works: Historical evidence suggests that exposing bad ideas to public scrutiny and counter-argument often proves more effective than suppression. Driving hate groups underground may actually strengthen them by allowing conspiracy theories about suppression to flourish.

Democratic Competence: A free society must trust citizens to evaluate competing ideas and reject harmful ones. Assuming that exposure to hate speech will automatically convert people to extremism reflects a paternalistic view inconsistent with democratic self-governance.

Transparency Enables Monitoring: When hate groups operate on major platforms subject to public scrutiny, law enforcement and civil society can better monitor potential threats and respond appropriately.

Implementation Framework

A common carrier approach to platform regulation might include:

Non-Discrimination Requirements: Platforms would be prohibited from removing, demoting, or restricting legal content based on its viewpoint or the identity of its speaker.

Transparent Processes: Any content removal would require clear legal justification, with robust appeals processes and public reporting requirements.

User Control: Instead of platform-imposed content filtering, users would receive powerful tools to customize their own experience, blocking or filtering content according to their personal preferences.

Safe Harbors: Platforms complying with common carrier obligations would receive enhanced protection from liability for user-generated content.

Economic and Practical Considerations

Some argue that forcing platforms to host all legal content would impose unreasonable costs or drive them out of business. However, this objection lacks merit for several reasons:

Reduced Moderation Costs: Eliminating subjective content decisions would actually reduce platforms' operational expenses by simplifying their moderation infrastructure.

Utility Model Viability: Common carriers like telephone companies have operated profitably for decades under non-discrimination requirements.

Public Value: If platforms provide essential public infrastructure, some regulatory costs may be justified as the price of doing business, similar to environmental or safety regulations in other industries.

Conclusion

The current system of private platform content moderation has failed to serve the public interest. It has created arbitrary censorship, suppressed legitimate discourse, and concentrated dangerous power over public speech in corporate hands.

Moving to a common carrier model for major platforms would restore consistency, protect democratic discourse, and ensure that the digital public square remains open to all voices. While this approach would require tolerating some speech that many find objectionable, this tolerance is the price of maintaining a free society.

The First Amendment's drafters understood that protecting popular speech requires no special effort—it is precisely the unpopular, challenging, and even offensive speech that most needs protection. In our digital age, extending these principles to the platforms that mediate most public discourse is not just prudent policy, but a democratic necessity.

Rather than allowing private corporations to make ad hoc decisions about acceptable speech, we should embrace legal frameworks that treat digital platforms like the public utilities they have become, ensuring that American principles of free expression survive and thrive in the digital age.

Once platforms begin removing content based on moral or political disapproval, the criteria for censorship inevitably expand. What begins with the removal of overt racism and violence soon extends to controversial political opinions, religious views, or even scientific debates. Twitter (now X) has banned users for questioning gender ideology, YouTube has demonetized or removed videos discussing COVID-19 origins, and Facebook has suppressed posts critical of government policies. The term "hate speech" is notoriously subjective. What one culture considers offensive, another may see as legitimate critique. For example:

1. The Common Carrier Principle

Historically, common carriers (such as telephone companies, postal services, and railroads) have been required to serve all customers without discrimination. This principle ensures that essential services do not become tools of oppression or monopoly. Social media platforms—Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Google—have become the digital equivalent of public utilities. Billions rely on them for communication, news, and commerce. Treating dominant online platforms as common carriers would not eliminate hateful ideas, but it would replace arbitrary private censorship with a public, legally defined boundary. When a company controls the “last mile” of public expression—deciding which posts reach the public in practice—its choices function less like ordinary business judgment and more like gatekeeping comparable to utilities, railroads, and telecommunications. For that reason, social media platforms and analogous online services should be legally required to host all lawful speech, subject only to clearly defined categories of illegality. This approach is not only consistent with a strong vision of free expression; it also aligns with the common carrier obligations that have historically governed intermediaries whose infrastructure is essential to public access.

Free Speech Is Not Just About Censorship by Government

Absolute free speech principles are often invoked to argue that the state may not criminalize or prohibit speech based on viewpoint. But the practical threat to free expression today increasingly comes not from government, but from private intermediaries acting as de facto publishers with enormous leverage. When platforms can label content “harmful,” “disruptive,” “deceptive,” or “unsafe” and thereby demote or remove it, they effectively determine which viewpoints get prominence and which are silenced—at a scale and speed that would be difficult to replicate through any ordinary editorial process.

A principled free speech commitment should therefore focus on preventing viewpoint discrimination by private gatekeepers who function as critical communication conduits. If the law’s core purpose is to protect the public’s access to ideas, it is a category error to assume that free expression only faces danger when the censor is the government. In a media ecosystem where the chokepoint is an algorithmic platform, the First Amendment value of open access can be honored only if the law limits the intermediary’s ability to suppress lawful speech.

Common Carrier Logic: When You Control Access, You Can’t Pick Viewpoints

Common carrier doctrine developed precisely because certain industries—telecommunications, railroads, postal services—are indispensable for communication and exchange. Their defining characteristic is not the neutrality of their “content,” but the fact that they must serve the public without discrimination based on private preferences. Where a carrier’s infrastructure is effectively the only practical means of reaching the public, allowing the carrier to act as a selective gatekeeper undermines democratic participation.

Social media platforms and large online services operate in a manner analogous to carriers. They provide the infrastructure for distributing speech to the public. In many contexts, a platform is not a mere publisher competing for readers; it is the marketplace’s essential roadway. If the roadway refuses entry to whole classes of speakers based on the viewpoint of their messages, the result is a private monopoly on access to public debate.

Thus, the common carrier obligation should apply to platforms as communication conduits: they should be required to transmit and host lawful content. The law should not force them to endorse content, but it should prevent them from excluding lawful speech categorically or by viewpoint.

“All Lawful Speech” Is the Right Boundary

The strongest version of this argument is straightforward: if the speech is lawful, it should be hosted. That boundary respects the civil-liberties commitment to protecting lawful expression, while also preserving the rule of law by permitting platforms to remove or refuse content that is genuinely illegal. The principle of “host all lawful content” does not require platforms to tolerate unlawful acts carried out through online systems. It requires that their role as access providers not become a substitute for legal adjudication.

A workable legal framework would therefore require platforms to:

  1. Host and distribute all lawful content, including expression that is unpopular or offensive, as long as it does not meet legally defined criteria for illegality.
  2. Remove content only pursuant to clear legal standards (e.g., court orders, verified statutory violations, or established notice-and-takedown procedures tied to specific categories of unlawful material).
  3. Provide prompt, auditable processes for challenges to takedowns or denials, including independent review where decisions are disputed.
  4. Avoid viewpoint discrimination—the distinguishing feature that converts an ordinary editorial decision into censorship by private power.

This approach is designed to prevent platforms from “outlawing” speech through private policy. It also preserves legitimate interests: platforms can protect against fraud, actual threats, harassment that meets legal elements, and other unlawful conduct. What they cannot do is decide—based on managerial preferences or moral disapproval—that certain viewpoints are unacceptable and therefore must be excluded.

Why Not Let Platforms Just Be Editors?

Some will argue that platforms should not be forced to carry speech because they are private entities entitled to speak—or to decline to speak—at will. But when private entities function as essential conduits, pure editorial autonomy becomes a form of privatized censorship that defeats the underlying purpose of free speech protections: enabling the public to receive information from a diversity of speakers.

More importantly, the “editor” analogy collapses when the service is used not merely to present an editorial product but as the primary distribution system for public discourse. A platform’s editorial discretion can be magnified beyond the boundaries of proportionality. Even if platforms retain other forms of expression—promoting their preferred content, labeling material, reducing reach for certain safety reasons—an outright refusal to host lawful speech is structurally different. It converts a communications pathway into a permission system, in which access depends on compliance with platform ideology rather than on legality.

The Policy Consequence: More Speech, Less Covert Censorship

A common carrier approach would yield immediate benefits for democratic participation:

  • Reduced covert censorship: Viewpoint suppression becomes harder when the law compels hosting of lawful speech.
  • More predictable rights: Speakers can rely on legality rather than on shifting terms of service.
  • Greater accountability: Platforms must justify removal decisions under objective standards rather than opaque policy rules.
  • Preservation of counter-speech: Lawful but offensive views can be contested publicly rather than erased privately.

Opponents may argue that such a regime would amplify extremist propaganda. But a regime centered on legality does not prevent counter-speech; it prevents the intermediary from acting as a censor. If a view is unlawful, the existing legal system can address it. If it is lawful, the public retains the ability to debate it—an outcome that is central to any robust free speech principle.

Conclusion: In a Public Marketplace, Access Should Not Be Conditional on Compliance

Platforms that function as the infrastructure of public communication should not be allowed to condition access to lawful speech on internal preferences, reputational calculations, or ideology. Free speech values are not served by delegating censorship authority to private firms whose incentives do not align with democratic openness. Under a common carrier framework, online services would be obligated to host and transmit all lawful content, subject to established legal boundaries and procedurally fair takedown rules.

This is not about forcing platforms to endorse messages; it is about preventing them from becoming a private government of the airwaves. When the law treats communication networks as carriers of lawful speech rather than as fiefdoms of discretionary exclusion, the public sphere becomes harder to silence—and democracy becomes easier to practice.
